title: Gases
note: The ideal gas law PV = nRT ties together pressure, volume, amount, and temperature, and contains Boyle's, Charles's, Gay-Lussac's, and Avogadro's laws as special cases. Temperatures must be in kelvin. In a mixture, each gas contributes its own partial pressure (Dalton's law), and lighter gases effuse faster (Graham's law).

read.title: One equation for every gas
text: Gases are mostly empty space. Their particles are tiny compared with the distances between them, and they move fast in straight lines until they collide. Because of this, gases of very different chemicals behave almost the same way, and one equation describes them all: PV = nRT.

Each older gas law is this equation with two variables held fixed. Hold n and T fixed and PV is constant, which is Boyle's law: squeeze a gas to half its volume and its pressure doubles. Hold n and P fixed and V is proportional to T, which is Charles's law. These proportions work only with kelvin temperatures, because 0 K is a true zero and 0 °C is not.

The equation also explains mixtures. In air, nitrogen, oxygen, and argon each push on the walls as if alone, and the total pressure is the sum of these partial pressures. A gas's share of the pressure equals its share of the moles.

Temperature sets the average kinetic energy of the particles, so at the same temperature light molecules move faster than heavy ones. That is why hydrogen effuses four times faster than oxygen: its molar mass is one-sixteenth as large, and rate depends on the square root. Gases stop behaving ideally at high pressure and low temperature, when the particles crowd together and attract each other.

q.q: Why must gas law calculations use kelvin?
o: Gas laws need a true zero of temperature

q.q: In a gas mixture, a component's partial pressure is set by
o: its mole fraction times the total pressure

q.q: Why does hydrogen effuse four times faster than oxygen?
o: Hydrogen molecules have more kinetic energy
